title: Initialization and Normalization
overview: Good initialization keeps activations and gradients at a sensible scale, and normalization layers keep them there during training. Together they make deep networks trainable.
objectives: Compute batch norm and layer norm
Choose a normalization for CNNs versus transformers

method.title: Variance preservation
method.body: Xavier init scales weights by 1/fan_avg and He init by 2/fan_in so signal variance stays stable across layers.

method.title: Batch norm
method.body: Normalizes each feature over the batch, then applies a learned scale and shift; it behaves differently at train and eval time.

method.title: Layer norm
method.body: Normalizes across features of a single example, so it is independent of batch size and standard in transformers.

method.title: Benefits
method.body: Allows higher learning rates and reduces sensitivity to initialization.

pseudocode:
# He init
W = randn(fan_in, fan_out) * sqrt(2 / fan_in)
# layer norm
mu = x.mean(-1); var = x.var(-1)
y = gamma * (x - mu) / sqrt(var + eps) + beta

playground.starterCode:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = rng.normal(5.0, 3.0, size=(4, 6))
mu = x.mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
var = x.var(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
y = (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + 1e-5)
print("row means:", np.round(y.mean(axis=-1), 3))
print("row stds: ", np.round(y.std(axis=-1), 3))
h = rng.normal(size=(1000, 256))
for name, scale in (("naive 0.01", 0.01), ("He", np.sqrt(2 / 256))):
    a = np.maximum(0, h @ (rng.normal(size=(256, 256)) * scale))
    print(name, "activation std:", round(float(a.std()), 3))
